steps.headingEn: Quick CLI Creation & Fail-Fast Validation Mindset (Python & Node.js)
steps.bodyEn:
In practice, when you want to avoid writing passwords to an intermediate YAML file on disk, you can create them directly from the command line using `--from-literal`:

```bash
kubectl create configmap app-cfg --from-literal=PORT=3000
kubectl create secret generic jwt-sec --from-literal=JWT_PUBLIC_KID=kid-2026
```

> [!TIP] Production pattern against silent failures: Validate env vars at startup (`Fail-Fast`)
> If you bulk-load an entire `ConfigMap` with `envFrom` and forget to define `REDIS_URL`, Kubernetes will still mark the Pod green as `1/1 Running`—only for it to crash with a `500` error when a customer clicks checkout! Always validate your env schema on the very first line of app startup:
> - **In Python (`FastAPI`):** Use **`pydantic-settings` (`BaseSettings`)** — missing required variables fail immediately with a crystal-clear `ValidationError` in `kubectl logs`!
> - **In Node.js / TypeScript:** Use **`zod`** (`envSchema.parse(process.env)`) at the top of `main.ts`!

```visual
kind: troubleshoot
title: Bảng Chẩn Đoán Sự Cố Cấu Hình ConfigMap & Secret Thực Chiến
items:
  - symptom: "Pod đứng im ở trạng thái 0/1 với STATUS: CreateContainerConfigError"
    badge: Chặn trước khi chạy
    tone: rose
    cause: "Pod tham chiếu tới một `Secret` hoặc `ConfigMap` chưa được tạo trên cùng Namespace, hoặc gõ sai tên khóa `key` trong `secretKeyRef` / `configMapKeyRef`."
    fix: "Xem dòng lỗi chính xác ở cuối bảng Events của lệnh describe, rồi tạo đúng Secret/ConfigMap còn thiếu."
    cmd: "kubectl describe pod billing-worker && kubectl get secret,cm"
  - symptom: "Pod vẫn báo 1/1 Running nhưng văng lỗi 500 giữa chừng khi có khách gọi API"
    badge: Bẫy thiếu biến envFrom
    tone: amber
    cause: "Dùng `envFrom` nạp sỉ cả `ConfigMap` mà bên trong vô tình thiếu mất khóa `REDIS_URL` — K8s vẫn cho container khởi chạy bình thường!"
    fix: "Áp dụng Fail-Fast Validation (`pydantic-settings` bên Python hoặc `zod` bên Node.js) ngay lúc khởi động để bắt lỗi tức thì qua `kubectl logs`."
    cmd: "kubectl logs deployment/shop-api"
```

> [!REMEMBER] Pocket Takeaways
> - **`ConfigMap`** (`data:`) stores public settings · **`Secret`** (`stringData:` → `data:`) stores sensitive data; **`Base64` is encoding, NOT encryption** — in Production use **External Secrets Operator** or **Sealed Secrets / SOPS**.
> - Bulk injection via **`envFrom`** (`configMapRef` / `secretRef`) **does not hot-reload** when a ConfigMap changes — you must run `kubectl rollout restart deployment/...`.
> - Referencing a missing Secret name or an invalid `key` in `secretKeyRef` blocks the Pod immediately in ==`CreateContainerConfigError`==.

readings.noteEn: Combines both techniques: bulk-loading env vars via envFrom and mounting a JSON config file via a read-only Volume.
readings.taskEn: Why did the author enable the `readOnly: true` flag in the `volumeMounts` configuration for `flags-vol`?
readings.answerEn: Setting `readOnly: true` prevents application code (or an attacker exploiting a file-write vulnerability) from modifying the configuration file inside the container, preserving immutability.

readings.noteEn: Direct root cause leading to the CreateContainerConfigError status.
readings.taskEn: Compare the key name in `Secret/billing-db-secret` with `secretKeyRef` in `Pod/billing-worker` to pinpoint the mismatch.
readings.answerEn: The Secret defines the key as `DATABASE_PASSWORD`, whereas the Pod specifies `key: DB_PASS`. When Kubelet assembles environment variables before starting the container and cannot find `DB_PASS`, it halts with `CreateContainerConfigError`.

K12-Q1.qEn: According to the 12-Factor App principle in Kubernetes, which data goes into a `ConfigMap` and which goes into a `Secret`?
choicesEn: Put everything directly into the `Dockerfile` using the `ENV` instruction
Non-sensitive settings (`LOG_LEVEL`, `CORS_ORIGIN`, `nginx.conf` files) go into `ConfigMap`; sensitive data (DB passwords, API keys, TLS certificates) go into `Secret`
`ConfigMap` only holds integers, while `Secret` only holds strings
`ConfigMap` is for Node.js, while `Secret` is only for Go
K12-Q1.explainEn: Separating public configuration (`ConfigMap`) from sensitive data (`Secret`) allows strict RBAC permissions and dedicated KMS encryption for `Secret` objects.

K12-Q2.qEn: Because the `data:` field of a Kubernetes `Secret` displays values as `Base64` strings, the data is cryptographically encrypted and safe to push in a `secret.yaml` file to a public Git repository.
K12-Q2.explainEn: Completely false! Base64 is merely a **character-representation encoding**, NOT cryptographic encryption — anyone can decode it back to plain text in seconds with `base64 -d`! Never commit unencrypted Secrets to Git.

K12-Q3.qEn: When you want to inject **all key-value pairs** from a `ConfigMap` named `api-config` as container environment variables (`process.env`) at once (instead of listing each key individually), which field do you use?
choicesEn: `envFrom: [{ configMapRef: { name: "api-config" } }]`
`imagePullSecrets: [{ name: "api-config" }]`
`ports: [{ name: "api-config" }]`
`selector: { configMap: "api-config" }`
K12-Q3.explainEn: `envFrom` bulk-injects every key from a `ConfigMap` (via `configMapRef`) or `Secret` (via `secretRef`) straight into `process.env`.

K12-Q4.qEn: A Pod references a `Secret` that has not been created in the cluster (or has a typo in `secretKeyRef`'s `key`). Before the container can even execute its first line of code, what characteristic long error name appears in the Pod's `STATUS` column?
K12-Q4.explainEn: `CreateContainerConfigError` indicates that Kubelet failed during the environment configuration setup step (a missing `ConfigMap` / `Secret` or key) prior to starting the container.

K12-Q5.qEn: In a `Secret` YAML manifest, which field allows you to write values as plain readable strings so the API Server automatically converts them to Base64 upon saving?
choicesEn: `rawBytes`
`stringData`
`plainText`
`clearData`
K12-Q5.explainEn: `stringData` is a write-only convenience field: you supply readable strings and Kubernetes automatically encodes them into Base64 under `data`.

K12-Q6.qEn: If you inject a `ConfigMap` into a Pod via environment variables (`env` / `envFrom`) and later update the `ConfigMap` values on the cluster, does `process.env` inside the running Pod automatically update right away?
choicesEn: Yes, `process.env` in Linux updates automatically after 1 millisecond
No! OS process environment variables are only loaded at container creation — you must restart the Pods (`kubectl rollout restart deployment/...`) to pick up the new values
The Pod will automatically delete the entire cluster
Node.js will automatically reinstall `npm ci`
K12-Q6.explainEn: Unlike Volume mounts (which can sync files automatically after ~1 minute), `process.env` environment variables are immutable for the lifetime of the process, requiring a Deployment `rollout restart`.

K12-Q7.qEn: In modern Production environments, instead of storing real passwords in Git repositories, teams commonly use **External Secrets Operator** (syncing from AWS Secrets Manager / HashiCorp Vault) or **Sealed Secrets / SOPS**.
K12-Q7.explainEn: Correct! This is the GitOps security gold standard in 2026 to achieve full automation while never exposing plain-text Secrets in Git.

K12-FC1.frontEn: What is the difference between injecting a `ConfigMap` with **`envFrom`** versus **`volumes`**?
K12-FC1.backEn:
- **`envFrom`:** Injects keys as `process.env` variables (requires a Pod restart when values change).
- **`volumes`:** Mounts keys as actual configuration files on the container's filesystem (e.g., `/etc/nginx/conf.d`).

K12-FC2.frontEn: Why do people say **"Base64 in a Kubernetes Secret is NOT security encryption"**?
K12-FC2.backEn: Because Base64 uses no secret key — anyone who can read the YAML can decode it back to plain text immediately using `base64 -d`. You must enable KMS Encryption at Rest and lock down RBAC.

K12-FC3.frontEn: What usually causes the **`CreateContainerConfigError`** status on a Pod?
K12-FC3.backEn: The Pod references a **`ConfigMap` or `Secret` that does not exist** in the same namespace, or specifies a **misspelled `key` name** in `configMapKeyRef` / `secretKeyRef`.

K12-FC4.frontEn: Which field in a `Secret` manifest lets you write plain-text strings without manually Base64-encoding them?

K12-FC5.frontEn: What is the CLI syntax to quickly create a `generic` Secret directly from key-value pairs?

K12-FC6.frontEn: When mounting a `ConfigMap` or `Secret` as `volumeMounts` in a container, which safety flag should you always enable?

K13.summaryEn: Dynamically provision disks via PVC & StorageClass, distinguish ReadWriteOnce vs ReadWriteMany, and operate databases with StatefulSet + Headless Service.

steps.headingEn: Overview & Context
steps.bodyEn:
At Level 0 and Level 1, when running PostgreSQL with Docker Compose on a single host, you simply declared `volumes: pgdata` sitting right on that machine's local hard drive. On a Kubernetes cluster of **15 Worker Nodes**, however, things get much more interesting:

- [>] Today your Pod runs on `worker-node-1`. Tonight `worker-node-1` undergoes hardware maintenance, so the `Scheduler` moves the Pod to `worker-node-8`.
- [!] If the data lived only on the local disk of `worker-node-1`, the new Pod on `worker-node-8` would wake up to an empty directory!

So that data can **"detach and follow the Pod"** regardless of which node it lands on, Kubernetes splits storage into 3 clean building blocks: `StorageClass`, `PersistentVolumeClaim (PVC)`, and `PersistentVolume (PV)` — paired with ==`StatefulSet`== for systems that require stable identities, such as databases.

steps.headingEn: Dynamic Disk Provisioning: StorageClass → PVC → PV
steps.bodyEn:
> [!NOTE] Role breakdown of the 3 storage objects: `StorageClass`, `PVC`, and `PV`
> Instead of forcing Python or Node.js developers to configure raw cloud disk IDs like AWS EBS `vol-0a1b2c3d`, Kubernetes separates storage provisioning into 3 independent objects:
> 1. **`StorageClass`:** Predefined by infrastructure engineers to describe cloud disk tiers (e.g., `gp3` for high-speed SSD, `efs` for shared network storage) along with reclaim policies.
> 2. **`PersistentVolumeClaim — PVC`:** The application's storage request slip (e.g., asking for `10Gi` of `storageClassName: gp3` with access mode `ReadWriteOnce`).
> 3. **`PersistentVolume — PV`:** The actual physical/cloud disk dynamically created by the **CSI Driver** upon receiving a `PVC`, then bound 1-to-1 (`Bound`) to that `PVC` (think of `StorageClass` as the catalog of disk tiers, `PVC` as the app's order form, and `PV` as the actual provisioned disk).

> [!WARNING] Classic pitfall leaving Pods stuck forever in `Pending`
> If in your `PVC` you mistype `storageClassName: ssd-nonexistent` (a tier missing from `kubectl get storageclass`), the `PVC` request will sit endlessly in `Pending` (never `Bound`), causing **every Pod mounting that `PVC` to also remain stuck in ==`Pending`==**, unable to start!

steps.headingEn: Mounting a PVC into a Pod or Deployment (volumes + volumeMounts)
steps.bodyEn:
Once you write a `PersistentVolumeClaim`, you attach it to your application in 2 familiar steps: declare the `volumes[].persistentVolumeClaim.claimName` source at the Pod level, and mount `volumeMounts[].mountPath` inside the Container:

```yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: PersistentVolumeClaim
metadata:
  name: upload-pvc
spec:
  storageClassName: gp3
  accessModes:
    - ReadWriteOnce
  resources:
    requests:
      storage: 10Gi
---
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: media-api
spec:
  replicas: 1
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: media-api
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: media-api
    spec:
      containers:
        - name: api
          image: ghcr.io/acme/media-api:1.2.0
          volumeMounts:
            - name: upload-storage
              mountPath: /app/uploads
      volumes:
        - name: upload-storage
          persistentVolumeClaim:
            claimName: upload-pvc
```

steps.headingEn: Why Databases Cannot Use Deployment and Require StatefulSet
steps.bodyEn:
For stateless Web APIs, replicas in a `Deployment` are completely interchangeable (`shop-api-7f8d9`, `shop-api-2x9k1`) — which replica starts or stops first makes no difference.

For a **PostgreSQL Primary – Replica** cluster, **Redis Cluster**, or **Kafka**, however, a `Deployment` fails due to 2 mandatory technical requirements:

- [!] **Cannot share a single binary disk:** If 2 PostgreSQL processes on 2 nodes write simultaneously to the same data directory, the database suffers immediate **data corruption**! Each database replica must have its **own dedicated `PVC`** bound exclusively to it.
- [!] **Requires sticky identity and ordinal ordering (*Sticky Identity*):** The primary `postgres-0` handles writes, while `postgres-1` acts as a Replica streaming from `postgres-0`'s exact address. If `postgres-0` restarts, it **must retain the exact name ==`postgres-0`== and reattach its original disk `data-postgres-0`**!

That is precisely why **`StatefulSet` (`apiVersion: apps/v1`)** exists:

steps.headingEn: Headless Service (clusterIP: None) & 2026 Production Advice
steps.bodyEn:
Every `StatefulSet` requires `spec.serviceName` to point to a **Headless Service** — a special `Service` configured with ==`spec.clusterIP: None`==. Seeing `clusterIP: None`, CoreDNS skips assigning a single virtual load-balancing IP and instead creates individual DNS records pointing directly to each replica:

- [x] `postgres-0.postgres-headless.default.svc.cluster.local` → Resolves directly to the primary instance **`postgres-0`** (handles `INSERT/UPDATE`)!
- [x] `postgres-1.postgres-headless.default.svc.cluster.local` → Resolves directly to the replica instance **`postgres-1`** (dedicated to read-only `SELECT` reporting queries)!

> [!TIP] 2026 Architecture Perspective: Managed DB or Self-Hosted DB on K8s?
> - If you run on AWS/GCP/Azure with a small team, using a managed database service (**AWS RDS**, **Cloud SQL**, **Neon**) outside the K8s cluster remains the lowest-maintenance way to get automated backups.
> - If you self-host on Kubernetes (On-Premise or for cloud cost optimization), rather than hand-crafting raw `StatefulSet` manifests for Postgres, teams in 2026 prefer dedicated Kubernetes Operators like **`CloudNativePG`** to automate both Primary-Replica failover and WAL backups to S3!

```visual
kind: troubleshoot
title: Hai Tình Huống Vận Hành Lưu Trữ Thường Gặp Trên Production

    fix: "Kiểm tra danh sách StorageClass thực tế của cụm và đối chiếu sự kiện chi tiết trên chiếc PVC."
    cmd: kubectl get storageclass && kubectl describe pvc upload-pvc
  - symptom: "Đã chạy kubectl delete statefulset postgres nhưng các PVC vẫn còn nguyên"
    badge: Cơ chế bảo vệ dữ liệu
    tone: emerald
    cause: "KHÔNG PHẢI LỖI! Khi xóa hoặc scale down `StatefulSet`, Kubernetes cố tình giữ lại toàn bộ `PVC` sinh từ `volumeClaimTemplates` để ngăn sự cố bấm nhầm xóa mất Database sản xuất."
    fix: "Nếu thực sự muốn dọn sạch ổ đĩa ở môi trường thử nghiệm, bạn phải xóa tường minh từng PVC sau khi đã sao lưu."
    cmd: kubectl get pvc && kubectl delete pvc data-postgres-0
```

> [!REMEMBER] Pocket Takeaways
> - **`ReadWriteOnce` (`RWO`)** = read-write mount for Pods on **a single Worker Node** (AWS EBS `gp3`) · **`ReadWriteMany` (`RWX`)** = simultaneous read-write across multiple Nodes over the network (EFS/NFS).
> - If a `PVC` is stuck in `Pending` (not `Bound`), any Pod mounting it will also stay in **`Pending`**.
> - **`StatefulSet`** numbers Pods starting from **`0`** (`postgres-0`), provisions per-Pod `PVC`s via **`volumeClaimTemplates`**, pairs with a **Headless Service (`spec.clusterIP: None`)**, and **does NOT auto-delete `PVC`s** when the `StatefulSet` is deleted!

readings.noteEn: Standard architecture for deploying PostgreSQL on K8s: combining a Headless Service (clusterIP: None) and a StatefulSet with per-replica volumeClaimTemplates.
readings.taskEn: Inspect the volumeClaimTemplates section and explain what happens to the data disks if you delete this StatefulSet.
readings.answerEn: Each Pod (postgres-0, postgres-1) automatically gets its own separate PVC generated from volumeClaimTemplates. When deleting the StatefulSet or scaling down replicas, Kubernetes INTENTIONALLY preserves those PVCs (never auto-deleting them) to protect database data safety.

readings.noteEn: Real-world error leaving both PVC and Pod stuck in Pending due to a typo in a non-existent StorageClass name.
readings.taskEn: Identify the misconfigured line in the PVC that prevents the CSI Provisioner from provisioning a disk for the application.
readings.answerEn: The storageClassName field is set to "fast-nvme-typo", which does not exist in the cluster's StorageClass list. You should check available classes with kubectl get storageclass and change it to a valid class like gp3 or standard.

K13-Q1.qEn: What does the `ReadWriteOnce` (`RWO`) access mode in a `PersistentVolumeClaim` accurately mean?
choicesEn: The disk allows data to be written only once ever, then becomes permanently read-only
The disk can be mounted in read-write mode by Pods running on the SAME single Worker Node at a time
The disk allows all Pods across 10 different Worker Nodes to write data simultaneously
The disk automatically wipes all data right after the Pod's first restart
K13-Q1.explainEn: ReadWriteOnce (RWO) mounts a block volume (like AWS EBS gp3) as read-write on 1 Worker Node at a time. Simultaneous multi-node read-write access requires ReadWriteMany (RWX) on network file storage such as EFS/NFS.

K13-Q2.qEn: When you delete a `StatefulSet` with `kubectl delete statefulset postgres`, Kubernetes automatically deletes all `PersistentVolumeClaim` objects created from `volumeClaimTemplates` to reclaim disk space.
K13-Q2.explainEn: False! By default, Kubernetes retains all StatefulSet PVCs even when the StatefulSet is deleted or scaled down, preventing catastrophic database data loss.

K13-Q3.qEn: For a `StatefulSet` named `postgres` with `replicas: 2`, what will the exact name of the first Pod created be?
K13-Q3.explainEn: Unlike Deployments that use random suffixes, a StatefulSet assigns deterministic ordinals starting at 0: postgres-0 is created first, and only once postgres-0 is Ready is postgres-1 created.

K13-Q4.qEn: To create a **Headless Service** providing individual DNS identities for each Pod in a `StatefulSet`, which `Service` field requires a special value?
choicesEn: spec.type: NodePort
spec.clusterIP: None
spec.headless: true
metadata.labels.headless: "yes"
K13-Q4.explainEn: Setting spec.clusterIP: None turns the Service into a Headless Service: K8s skips allocating a shared load-balanced Virtual IP and returns direct DNS A records for each Pod (e.g., postgres-0.postgres-headless...).

K13-Q5.qEn: Why should a database cluster like PostgreSQL Primary-Replica NOT use a `Deployment` sharing a single `PVC`?
choicesEn: Because Deployment does not support injecting Secret environment variables
Because multiple database processes writing concurrently to the same binary data directory causes data corruption, and databases require stable network identities per node
Because Deployment only supports a maximum of 1 replica
Because Deployment does not support TCP port 5432
K13-Q5.explainEn: Each database node needs an independent data disk (via volumeClaimTemplates) and a stable ordinal identity (postgres-0 as Primary, postgres-1 as Replica) — capabilities only StatefulSet provides.

K13-Q6.qEn: If a Pod declares a `PersistentVolumeClaim` mount while that `PVC` is stuck in `Pending` (not yet `Bound` to a `PV`), the Pod itself will also remain held in `Pending` unable to run.
K13-Q6.explainEn: True! Neither the scheduler nor kubelet can start the container until its required storage volume has been provisioned and successfully bound.

K13-Q7.qEn: In the configuration below, at which absolute directory path inside the container will the Node.js application read and write uploaded files?
K13-Q7.explainEn: The volumeMounts[].mountPath field specifies the directory path inside the container's filesystem mapped to the external PVC.

K13-C1.frontEn: How do the roles of `StorageClass`, `PersistentVolumeClaim (PVC)`, and `PersistentVolume (PV)` differ?
K13-C1.backEn: `StorageClass` defines disk tiers (like `gp3`), `PVC` is the application's storage request slip, and `PV` is the actual disk dynamically provisioned by the CSI Driver and bound 1:1 with the `PVC`.

K13-C2.frontEn: What is the core difference between `ReadWriteOnce (RWO)` and `ReadWriteMany (RWX)`?
K13-C2.backEn: `RWO` allows read-write mounting on only 1 Worker Node at a time (EBS/PD block storage); `RWX` allows multiple Pods across multiple Nodes to read and write concurrently (EFS/NFS/CephFS network storage).

K13-C3.frontEn: What three characteristics make `StatefulSet` fundamentally different from `Deployment`?
K13-C3.backEn: 1) Deterministic ordinal Pod names (`0, 1, 2...`), 2) Strict sequential startup and teardown, 3) `volumeClaimTemplates` that automatically provision an independent PVC per Pod.

K13-C4.frontEn: What is a Headless Service and how is it written in YAML?
K13-C4.backEn: A `Service` with `spec.clusterIP: None` that skips load-balancing virtual IPs and creates DNS records pointing directly to each `StatefulSet` Pod (`<pod-name>.<svc-name>.<ns>.svc.cluster.local`).

K13-C5.frontEn: What are the most common reasons a `PVC` gets stuck in `Pending`?
K13-C5.backEn: `storageClassName` references a storage class that does not exist on the cluster, the matching CSI Driver is not installed, or cloud disk quota is exhausted.

K13-C6.frontEn: What happens to data in PVCs when a `StatefulSet` is deleted?
K13-C6.backEn: The `PVC`s remain intact (they are not automatically deleted) to protect data; recreating a `StatefulSet` with the same name automatically reattaches `postgres-0` to its original `postgres-0` disk.

K14.titleEn: Pod Health Checks (Startup / Readiness / Liveness Probes) & Graceful Shutdown
K14.summaryEn: Clearly distinguish the 3 Health Probes, prevent cascading failures from database checks in livenessProbe, and configure zero-downtime Pod termination with preStop + SIGTERM.

steps.headingEn: Overview & Context
steps.bodyEn:
One of the most common misconceptions among Kubernetes newcomers is: *"As long as `kubectl get pods` reports `STATUS = Running`, my Python or Node.js application is ready to serve customers!"*

**Not necessarily!** To the Linux kernel and `kubelet`, `Running` simply means the `uvicorn` or `node` process was just loaded into RAM (its PID has started). In reality:

- [!] A FastAPI service loading an AI model into RAM (or a Node.js app establishing PostgreSQL / Redis connection pools) may take 10–30 seconds to initialize — routing traffic to it at second 1 immediately returns **`502 Bad Gateway`**!
- [!] After running continuously for days, an app can hit a *Deadlock* where every request hangs indefinitely even though the process hasn't exited (a false `Running` state)!

To help Kubernetes accurately understand the application's internal heartbeat, we equip it with **3 health-check sensors (`startupProbe`, `readinessProbe`, `livenessProbe`)** combined with ==Graceful Shutdown (`preStop` + `SIGTERM`)==.

steps.headingEn: Distinguishing the 3 Probes: startupProbe, readinessProbe, and livenessProbe
steps.bodyEn:
> [!NOTE] Roles of the 3 Health Probe types in Kubernetes
> Each Probe inspects a different lifecycle phase and triggers a different action from `kubelet`:
> 1. **`startupProbe`:** Protects applications with slow initial startup times (e.g., 30–60s to load AI models or warm caches). Until `startupProbe` succeeds, `kubelet` temporarily disables `livenessProbe` and `readinessProbe` so it doesn't prematurely kill the container.
> 2. **`readinessProbe`:** Checks whether the Pod is currently fit to receive new traffic from a `Service`. If it fails, `kubelet` only marks `Ready=false` to remove the Pod's IP from the `Service`'s `Endpoints` list—**it never restarts the container**.
> 3. **`livenessProbe`:** Checks whether the application process is still healthy or stuck in a *deadlock*. If consecutive failures exceed `failureThreshold`, `kubelet` **restarts the container (`RESTARTS +1`)**.
> *(Think of it simply: `startupProbe` is the initial morning warm-up time, `readinessProbe` temporarily puts up a "paused for new orders" sign when overloaded without shutting down, and `livenessProbe` checks for a frozen process to trigger a reboot.)*

steps.headingEn: Critical Mistake to Avoid: Checking the Database in livenessProbe
steps.bodyEn:
Consider a real incident pattern that has caused widespread outages across large systems when developers point both `readinessProbe` and `livenessProbe` at a shared `/health` route running `SELECT 1` against PostgreSQL (with `timeoutSeconds: 1`):

1. During peak hours, PostgreSQL gets busy and takes `1.3 seconds` to respond to `SELECT 1` (exceeding the `1s` threshold).
2. `livenessProbe` fails 3 times → Kubernetes assumes all 20 API Pods are deadlocked and **simultaneously kills and restarts all 20 Pods at once**!
3. When all 20 FastAPI / Node.js Pods boot back up together, they slam the struggling PostgreSQL instance with 200 brand-new TCP connections (**Thundering Herd** effect), taking down the database completely and plunging the whole cluster into a ==cascading `CrashLoopBackOff` (*Cascading Failure*)==!

```visual
kind: compare
title: "Nguyên Tắc Vàng: Tách Bạch /healthz (Liveness) và /readyz (Readiness)"
subtitle: Phụ thuộc bên ngoài (PostgreSQL, Redis, API đối tác) CHỈ ĐƯỢC KIỂM TRA ở readinessProbe!
left:
  badge: "CÁCH SAI · Sập Dây Chuyền"
  title: Nhét kiểm tra Database vào livenessProbe
  tone: rose
  code: |
    # SAI LẦM NGHIÊM TRỌNG: DB chập chờn 2s -> K8s giết sạch 20 Pod API!
    livenessProbe:
      httpGet:
        path: /readyz-with-db-query
        port: 3000
      timeoutSeconds: 1
      failureThreshold: 3
  lang: yaml
  bullets:
    - "PostgreSQL hoặc cổng thanh toán đối tác chỉ chậm nhẹ vài giây cũng làm `livenessProbe` thất bại"
    - "K8s tự tay giết toàn bộ dàn API đang sống khỏe, gây bão kết nối **Thundering Herd** lúc bật lại"
right:
  badge: "CÁCH CHUẨN · Cô Lập Sự Cố"
  title: "/healthz nội tại nhẹ nhàng · /readyz kiểm tra kết nối"
  tone: emerald
  code: |
    readinessProbe:
      httpGet: { path: /readyz, port: 3000 }  # Check DB/Redis Pool
      periodSeconds: 5
      failureThreshold: 3
    livenessProbe:
      httpGet: { path: /healthz, port: 3000 } # Chỉ trả 200 {"ok": true}!
      periodSeconds: 10
      timeoutSeconds: 3
      failureThreshold: 3
  lang: yaml
  bullets:
    - "**`/healthz` (`livenessProbe` & `startupProbe`):** Chỉ trả về ngay `200 {\"ok\": true}` chứng minh tiến trình chưa bị đơ cứng, **không chạm DB/Redis/API ngoài**"
    - "**`/readyz` (`readinessProbe`):** Kiểm tra kết nối DB/Redis; khi DB chập chờn chỉ tạm rút Pod khỏi `Service`, không giết Pod!"
```

The gold-standard production configuration combining all 3 Probes:

```yaml
containers:
  - name: api
    image: ghcr.io/acme/shop-api:1.5.0
    ports:
      - containerPort: 3000
    startupProbe:
      httpGet:
        path: /healthz
        port: 3000
      periodSeconds: 5
      failureThreshold: 12    # Tổng quỹ thời gian khởi động tối đa = 5 * 12 = 60 giây
    readinessProbe:
      httpGet:
        path: /readyz
        port: 3000
      periodSeconds: 5
      failureThreshold: 3
    livenessProbe:
      httpGet:
        path: /healthz        # Nhẹ nhàng, tuyệt đối không gọi DB ngoài!
        port: 3000
      periodSeconds: 10
      timeoutSeconds: 3
      failureThreshold: 3
```

steps.headingEn: Zero-Downtime Pod Termination: Handling Terminating with preStop Hook and SIGTERM
steps.bodyEn:
Even with `readinessProbe` configured, many teams still see occasional `502 Bad Gateway` errors during the first few seconds of a Rolling Update! The cause lies in **two asynchronous parallel flows** triggered the instant Kubernetes deletes an old Pod:

- [>] **Flow A (Cluster Networking):** The API Server notifies `EndpointSlice`, `kube-proxy`, and the `Ingress / Gateway Controller` to remove the old Pod's IP from load-balancer tables. Network propagation takes roughly **1 to 3 seconds**.
- [!] **Flow B (`kubelet` on the Node):** At that exact same moment, `kubelet` sends **`SIGTERM`** straight to the application process! If Uvicorn or Express immediately closes its HTTP listening port within `0.05 seconds` upon receiving `SIGTERM`, in-flight client packets still arriving from Flow A slam into a closed socket → **`502 Bad Gateway`**!

```visual
kind: flow
title: Chu Trình Dừng An Toàn Không Rớt Mạng (Zero-Downtime Graceful Shutdown)
subtitle: "Toàn bộ preStop + SIGTERM đều nằm chung bên trong tổng quỹ thời gian terminationGracePeriodSeconds (mặc định 30s)"
footer: "Nếu preStop ngủ 5s trong quỹ 30s, ứng dụng (FastAPI lifespan / Node server.close) còn tối đa 25s để xử lý nốt request cũ trước khi bị bắn SIGKILL"
steps:
  - icon: network
    badge: Giây 0 · Song song
    title: Pod Terminating & Gỡ IP
    desc: Luồng mạng bắt đầu rút IP của Pod khỏi EndpointSlice và Gateway/Ingress (mất ~1-3s)
    code: "Ready -> Terminating"
    tone: sky
    edge: chạy preStop trước
  - icon: shield
    badge: Giây 0 -> 5 · Đệm mạng
    title: lifecycle.preStop
    desc: Chạy TRƯỚC KHI gửi SIGTERM để chờ mạng cụm ngừng hẳn việc đẩy khách mới vào
    code: '["sh", "-c", "sleep 5"]'
    tone: amber
    edge: gửi SIGTERM
  - icon: check
    badge: Giây 5+ · Xả giao dịch
    title: Bắt SIGTERM & Đóng Êm
    desc: Uvicorn lifespan / Node server.close() hoàn tất nốt giao dịch dở dang rồi đóng DB
    code: "Exit Code 0"
    tone: emerald
    edge: nếu lố 30s ân hạn
  - icon: flame
    badge: Quá hạn 30s · Cưỡng bức
    title: Tín hiệu SIGKILL (9)
    desc: Nhân Linux/kubelet kết liễu cưỡng bức nếu tiến trình vẫn treo quá hạn ân hạn
    code: "SIGKILL"
    tone: rose
```

> [!TIP] `terminationGracePeriodSeconds` Budget Rule & Distroless Note
> - Execution time of the `lifecycle.preStop` hook is **counted inside** the total `terminationGracePeriodSeconds: 30` budget (for example, if `preStop` sleeps `5s`, the app has `25s` left to drain requests after `SIGTERM` before receiving ==`SIGKILL`==).
> - Since Kubernetes v1.30+, in addition to shell commands like `["sh", "-c", "sleep 5"]`, K8s natively supports `preStop: { sleep: { seconds: 5 } }` — super convenient for minimal Distroless containers without `/bin/sh`!

> [!REMEMBER] Pocket Takeaways
> - **`startupProbe`** holds off `liveness` & `readiness` during initial boot (max startup budget = **`periodSeconds * failureThreshold`**).
> - A failing **`readinessProbe`** **never kills a Pod**, it only removes its IP from `Service Endpoints` · **Only check external DB/APIs in `readinessProbe`**, never in `livenessProbe`!
> - Combine **`lifecycle.preStop`** + handling **`SIGTERM`** within the **`terminationGracePeriodSeconds`** budget (exceeding it results in a forced **`SIGKILL`**).

readings.noteEn: Production gold-standard blueprint for a Node.js service: separating all 3 Probe types and adding a 5-second preStop sleep hook to drain connections cleanly.
readings.taskEn: Read the lifecycle.preStop section and explain why sleep 5 is needed before the Node.js application receives the SIGTERM signal.
readings.answerEn: When a Pod enters Terminating, EndpointSlice/Ingress takes 1–3 seconds to update routing tables across the cluster. Running sleep 5 in preStop keeps the app's port open to finish handling late in-flight requests, preventing 502 Bad Gateway errors.

readings.noteEn: Common production anti-pattern: embedding a Database health query inside livenessProbe with a 1-second timeout, causing a system-wide cascading failure.
readings.taskEn: Explain what happens to all 10 API Pods if the Database experiences a temporary 1.5-second slowdown.
readings.answerEn: All 10 Pods simultaneously fail livenessProbe after 3 cycles and get killed by kubelet at the exact same time! When they restart together, all 10 Pods flood the Database with new connections (Thundering Herd), triggering a full CrashLoopBackOff outage. DB checks belong exclusively in readinessProbe!

K14-Q1.qEn: What is Kubernetes' exact action when a Pod's `readinessProbe` fails consecutively beyond `failureThreshold`?
choicesEn: Immediately kill the container with SIGKILL and increment the RESTARTS column by 1
Permanently delete the Deployment owning that Pod
Keep the Pod running but temporarily remove its IP from the Service's Endpoints list to stop sending new traffic to it
Automatically double the Pod's RAM memory limit
K14-Q1.explainEn: readinessProbe NEVER kills a Pod! It only marks the Pod Ready=false and removes its IP from Service Endpoints until the application recovers and passes the check again.

K14-Q2.qEn: A best practice for Node.js apps is pointing `livenessProbe` at an endpoint that queries all external dependencies (PostgreSQL, Redis, third-party payment gateways) to ensure the whole system is healthy.
K14-Q2.explainEn: Completely false! Putting external DB/API checks in livenessProbe causes Cascading Failures: a brief hiccup in a partner API or DB will make K8s kill your entire API fleet! External dependencies belong only in readinessProbe.

K14-Q3.qEn: Given the `startupProbe` configuration below, what is the maximum total time budget in seconds the application has to finish initial startup before `kubelet` considers it failed? (Enter an integer only)
K14-Q3.explainEn: The maximum startup budget of startupProbe is calculated as periodSeconds * failureThreshold = 5 * 12 = 60 seconds.

K14-Q4.qEn: While `startupProbe` is still checking a newly started container (before its first success), what is the state of `livenessProbe` and `readinessProbe`?
choicesEn: All three run concurrently starting at second 0
livenessProbe and readinessProbe are completely disabled until startupProbe succeeds for the first time
livenessProbe is permanently deleted from the Pod
readinessProbe automatically flips to Ready=true immediately
K14-Q4.explainEn: startupProbe exists to protect slow-starting apps: until it passes for the first time, kubelet suppresses livenessProbe so an app loading data isn't killed prematurely.

K14-Q5.qEn: Why should production API Pods configure a `lifecycle.preStop` hook running `["sh", "-c", "sleep 5"]`?
choicesEn: To make logs look nicer before the container shuts down
To give Service/Ingress routing tables across Nodes time to fully remove the Pod's IP before the Node.js process receives SIGTERM and closes its listening port
To save 5% on cloud CPU billing
Because Node.js does not support catching SIGTERM
K14-Q5.explainEn: Endpoint removal across the cluster network runs asynchronously in parallel with Pod termination on the Node. A 5-second sleep buffer in preStop eliminates 502 errors for late in-flight client packets.

K14-Q6.qEn: The execution duration of the `lifecycle.preStop` hook is counted inside the total `terminationGracePeriodSeconds` limit (30 seconds by default), rather than added on top of it.
K14-Q6.explainEn: True! If terminationGracePeriodSeconds is 30s and preStop sleeps for 25s, the application has only 5s left after receiving SIGTERM to close connections before being hit with SIGKILL.

K14-Q7.qEn: When a Pod exceeds `terminationGracePeriodSeconds` and its process still refuses to exit after `SIGTERM`, what forceful signal does the Linux kernel/kubelet send to terminate it?
K14-Q7.explainEn: Once the grace period expires without the process stopping after SIGTERM, the system sends SIGKILL (signal 9, which cannot be caught or ignored) to reclaim resources immediately.

K14-C1.frontEn: What is the decisive difference between `readinessProbe` and `livenessProbe` on failure?
K14-C1.backEn: A failing `readinessProbe` only removes the Pod from the `Service`'s traffic pool (without killing it); a failing `livenessProbe` kills and restarts the container.

K14-C2.frontEn: When should you use `startupProbe` instead of increasing `initialDelaySeconds` on `livenessProbe`?
K14-C2.backEn: When an app takes a long time on initial boot (30–90s) but needs fast deadlock detection once running (every 10s). Startup budget formula: `periodSeconds * failureThreshold`.

K14-C3.frontEn: Why is checking Database connectivity inside `livenessProbe` FORBIDDEN?
K14-C3.backEn: Because a brief DB slowdown will cause `livenessProbe` to kill all API Pods simultaneously, triggering a connection storm (Thundering Herd) and cascading outage when they all reboot together.

K14-C4.frontEn: What is the sequence of events when Kubernetes deletes a Pod (Graceful Termination)?
K14-C4.backEn: 1) Mark `Terminating` & remove IP from `Endpoints` (in parallel), 2) Run `lifecycle.preStop`, 3) Send `SIGTERM` to PID 1, 4) Send `SIGKILL` if still running after `terminationGracePeriodSeconds`.

K14-C5.frontEn: What is the role of `preStop: sleep 5` for a Node.js app behind an Ingress?
K14-C5.backEn: Provides a 5-second buffer so `kube-proxy` and the `Ingress Controller` finish updating Pod endpoint lists cluster-wide before Express/Fastify closes its TCP socket, eliminating `502` errors during deploys.

K14-C6.frontEn: What are the three probe check mechanisms supported by Kubernetes?
K14-C6.backEn: 1) `httpGet` (HTTP status `200..399` passes), 2) `tcpSocket` (TCP port handshake succeeds), 3) `exec` (command inside container exits with code `0`) — plus `grpc` for gRPC services.

kube-ex-k14-1.titleEn: Add a readinessProbe to Prevent Routing Traffic to Unready Pods
kube-ex-k14-1.promptEn:
The `shop-api` app takes about 4 seconds at startup to initialize database connections, after which it returns HTTP 200 at `/readyz` on port `3000`.

Add a `readinessProbe` to the `api` container in the `Deployment` with:
- `httpGet.path: /readyz`
- `httpGet.port: 3000`
- `periodSeconds: 5`
hintsEn: `readinessProbe:` goes directly inside the `- name: api` container block (at the same level as `image` and `ports`).
Ensure `port: 3000` is an integer (without quotation marks).

kube-ex-k14-2.titleEn: Add a livenessProbe to Automatically Restart Frozen Processes
kube-ex-k14-2.promptEn:
Add a `livenessProbe` sensor to the `api` container so that if the Node.js Event Loop freezes, `kubelet` automatically restarts it:

- `httpGet.path: /healthz`
- `httpGet.port: 3000`
- `periodSeconds: 10`
- `failureThreshold: 3`
hintsEn: The structure of `livenessProbe` matches `readinessProbe`, with an `httpGet` sub-block and timing fields at the same indentation level as `httpGet`.

kube-ex-k14-3.titleEn: Protect a Slow-Starting App with startupProbe (60s Budget)
kube-ex-k14-3.promptEn:
The `reco-engine` product recommendation service takes up to **45 seconds** to load its data index into memory on boot, causing `livenessProbe` to keep killing it prematurely!

Keep the responsive `livenessProbe` intact and add a **`startupProbe`** to the `reco` container:
- `httpGet.path: /healthz`, `httpGet.port: 3000`
- `periodSeconds: 5`
- `failureThreshold: 12` *(creates a safe `5 * 12 = 60 second` budget)*
hintsEn: Place the `startupProbe:` block at the same indentation level as `livenessProbe:` inside the `- name: reco` container.

kube-ex-k14-4.titleEn: Fix Cascading Failure Trap Caused by Database Check in livenessProbe
kube-ex-k14-4.promptEn:
The configuration below has a critical architectural flaw: `livenessProbe` hits `/readyz?check_db=true` with `timeoutSeconds: 1`, and `readinessProbe` is missing altogether! Whenever PostgreSQL takes longer than 1 second, the entire API fleet gets killed at once.

Fix it to follow production best practices:
1. Change `livenessProbe.httpGet.path` to the lightweight internal **`/healthz`** endpoint (without `check_db`) and raise `livenessProbe.timeoutSeconds` to at least `3`.
2. Add a new **`readinessProbe`** checking `httpGet.path: /readyz` on `port: 3000` (`periodSeconds: 5`).
hintsEn: Update `livenessProbe.httpGet.path` to `/healthz` and change `timeoutSeconds: 1` to `3`.
Add a `readinessProbe` block checking `httpGet.path: /readyz` and `port: 3000`.

kube-ex-k14-5.titleEn: Configure Graceful Pod Shutdown with preStop Hook and terminationGracePeriodSeconds
kube-ex-k14-5.promptEn:
Every time a new version of `checkout-api` is deployed, users hit a few `502 Bad Gateway` errors because Pods close their ports faster than Ingress updates its routes.

Configure Graceful Shutdown for the `Deployment`:
1. At the Pod level (`spec.template.spec`): set `terminationGracePeriodSeconds: 30`.
2. At the Container level (`spec.template.spec.containers[0]`): add `lifecycle.preStop.exec.command` as the array `["sh", "-c", "sleep 5"]`.
hintsEn: Watch the indentation: `terminationGracePeriodSeconds: 30` belongs under `spec.template.spec` (aligned with `containers:`).
Meanwhile, `lifecycle:` goes inside the `- name: api` container item. You can write `command: ["sh", "-c", "sleep 5"]` on a single line for brevity!

K15.summaryEn: Configure accurate requests/limits quotas, classify QoS tiers, autoscale with autoscaling/v2 HPA, and run one-off migrations or scheduled reports via Job & CronJob.

steps.headingEn: Overview & Context
steps.bodyEn:
On a personal computer, a Python or Node.js process can freely consume as much CPU and RAM as it wants. However, on a shared Kubernetes cluster where 40 services share Worker Node resources, a single data-processing worker with a memory leak or massive JSON calculation can exhaust the entire server's memory, taking down critical payment services running on the same Node!

In this lesson, you will master the three pillars of Kubernetes capacity management: **`resources` (`requests` vs `limits`) & QoS**, automatic scaling based on real-time load with ==`HorizontalPodAutoscaler` (`autoscaling/v2`)==, and running one-off / scheduled tasks with **`Job` & `CronJob` (`batch/v1`)**.

```visual

src: "/illustrations/kube/k8s-oom-vs-throttling.jpg"
alt: "So sánh CPU Throttling với Memory OOMKilled (Exit Code 137), cơ chế tự động co giãn HPA v2 và tác vụ định kỳ Job/CronJob"

caption: "Sự khác biệt quan trọng giữa vượt trần CPU (chỉ hãm xung) và vượt trần RAM (bị giết OOM 137), vòng lặp co giãn HPA v2 và lịch trình CronJob"

    tone: amber
```

steps.headingEn: Distinguishing resources.requests and resources.limits
steps.bodyEn:
> [!NOTE] Distinguishing `resources.requests` (guaranteed minimum) and `resources.limits` (maximum cap)
> - **`resources.requests`:** The minimum amount of resources a Pod asks to be allocated. **`kube-scheduler`** relies solely on `requests` to find a Worker Node with enough available capacity to schedule the Pod, and HPA also uses `requests` as the denominator when calculating load percentage.
> - **`resources.limits`:** The maximum consumption threshold a container is not allowed to exceed during actual execution, enforced directly by Linux kernel **`cgroups`**. If the Node has spare resources, the Pod is allowed to burst above `requests` but will be stopped at the `limits` ceiling. *(Think of `requests` as reserved seating for the Scheduler to place the Pod on a Node, and `limits` as the maximum circuit breaker during operation.)*

Kubernetes measurement units:
- [>] **CPU is measured in Millicores (`m`):** `1000m = 1 vCPU` (1 full virtual core) → **`500m = 0.5 vCPU`**, **`250m = 0.25 vCPU`**.
- [>] **RAM is measured in powers of 2 (`Mi`, `Gi`):** **`256Mi`** (*Mebibytes*), `512Mi`, `1Gi = 1024Mi` (always include the `i` in `Mi` / `Gi` to make binary units explicit!).

```visual
kind: compare
title: "So Sánh resources.requests (Đặt Chỗ) vs resources.limits (Giới Hạn Cứng)"
subtitle: Một bên phục vụ xếp lịch chỗ ngồi trên Control Plane, một bên do nhân Linux cưỡng chế lúc đang chạy!
left:
  badge: "kube-scheduler ĐỌC · Đặt Chỗ"
  title: resources.requests (Mức đảm bảo tối thiểu)
  tone: sky
  code: |
    resources:
      requests:
        cpu: "250m"      # Giữ chỗ 0.25 vCPU
        memory: "256Mi"  # Giữ chỗ 256 Mebibytes RAM
  lang: yaml
  bullets:
    - "Thành phần ==`kube-scheduler`== dùng con số `requests` để tìm Worker Node còn đủ chỗ trống xếp cho Pod mới"
    - "Đồng thời **HPA dùng chính `requests`** làm mẫu số để tính phần trăm tải!"
    - "Nếu không Node nào trên cụm còn trống đủ `requests`, Pod đứng chờ ở trạng thái **`Pending`**"
right:
  badge: "Linux cgroups CƯỠNG CHẾ · Trần Tối Đa"
  title: resources.limits (Giới hạn cứng không thể vượt)
  tone: amber
  code: |
    resources:
      limits:
        cpu: "500m"      # Trần 0.5 vCPU -> Vượt bị Throttling
        memory: "512Mi"  # Trần 512Mi -> Vượt bị OOMKilled (137)!
  lang: yaml
  bullets:
    - "**Vượt `limits.cpu`:** CPU là tài nguyên nén được nên chỉ bị ==hãm xung nhịp (`CPU Throttling`)== — phản hồi chậm đi đôi chút nhưng **KHÔNG bị giết**"
    - "**Vượt `limits.memory`:** RAM không thể nén nên nhân Linux kích hoạt **OOM Killer**, bắn chết container ngay lập tức với ==`OOMKilled` (`Exit Code 137`)==!"
```

> [!TIP] Production `limits` best practices (2026) for Python & Node.js
> - **For RAM:** Always set `requests.memory` close to realistic baseline usage and `limits.memory` with ~25–40% headroom for short traffic spikes (for Node.js, set `NODE_OPTIONS="--max-old-space-size=..."` to ~75% of the limit; for Python AI/Pandas, carefully calculate the size of models loaded into RAM).
> - **For CPU:** Do not clamp `limits.cpu` too low (e.g., `100m`), because during startup a FastAPI / TypeScript application needs a burst to load hundreds of modules—clamping too tightly triggers *CPU Throttling* and makes startup 5x slower!

steps.headingEn: Priority mechanism when a Node runs out of RAM: **3 QoS Classes**
steps.bodyEn:
Based on how you declare `requests` and `limits`, Kubernetes automatically classifies each Pod into one of 3 **Quality of Service (QoS)** classes. When a Worker Node unexpectedly runs out of physical RAM, `kubelet` uses this QoS class to determine the Pod eviction order (*Eviction*) to reclaim memory for the system:

```visual
kind: groups
title: 3 Hạng QoS Classes Khi Worker Node Thiếu Bộ Nhớ
subtitle: Thứ tự bị trục xuất khỏi Node (Eviction) đi từ BestEffort -> Burstable -> Guaranteed
columns: 3
items:
  - num: 1
    icon: trash
    title: BestEffort
    badge: Bị đuổi ĐẦU TIÊN
    tone: rose
    desc: Mức ưu tiên thấp nhất khi không khai báo tài nguyên.
    bullets:
      - "Hoàn toàn **không khai báo** bất kỳ `requests` hay `limits` nào"
      - "Khi máy chủ thiếu RAM vật lý, nhóm này bị loại bỏ đầu tiên ngay lập tức"
    footer: Chỉ dùng cho job nháp thử nghiệm không quan trọng
  - num: 2
    icon: activity
    title: Burstable
    badge: Linh hoạt · Phổ biến nhất
    tone: sky
    desc: Đặt mức nền vừa phải, cho phép dùng thêm khi Node còn dư tài nguyên.
    bullets:
      - "Khai báo `requests` **nhỏ hơn** `limits` (ví dụ `requests: 256Mi`, `limits: 512Mi`)"
      - "Bình thường tiết kiệm chi phí Node, lúc đông khách được phép tăng tốc lên tới `limits`"
    footer: Tiêu chuẩn cho phần lớn Web / FastAPI / Node REST API
  - num: 3
    icon: shield-check
    title: Guaranteed
    badge: Ưu tiên cao nhất
    tone: emerald
    desc: Mức bảo vệ cao nhất cho các dịch vụ lõi quan trọng.
    bullets:
      - "**Mọi container trong Pod** đều khai báo cả CPU lẫn Memory sao cho ==`requests` bằng khít tuyệt đối `limits`== (`cpu: 500m`, `memory: 512Mi`)"
      - "Được bảo vệ tới cùng, gần như không bao giờ bị trục xuất khỏi Node"
    footer: Dành riêng cho Database & cổng thanh toán payment-core
```

steps.headingEn: Autoscaling on real traffic: HorizontalPodAutoscaler (autoscaling/v2)
steps.bodyEn:
Instead of staying up at night manually running `kubectl scale` during every Flash Sale and scaling down manually the next morning to save Cloud costs, **`HorizontalPodAutoscaler` (HPA)** continuously reads real-time metrics from **Metrics Server** every 15 seconds and automatically scales the `Deployment`'s `replicas` up or down:

```yaml
apiVersion: autoscaling/v2
kind: HorizontalPodAutoscaler
metadata:
  name: shop-api-hpa
spec:
  scaleTargetRef:
    apiVersion: apps/v1
    kind: Deployment
    name: shop-api
  minReplicas: 2
  maxReplicas: 10
  metrics:
    - type: Resource
      resource:
        name: cpu
        target:
          type: Utilization
          averageUtilization: 70
```

> [!WARNING] Mandatory prerequisite for HPA to work!
> The `averageUtilization: 70` value is calculated by HPA as `(average actual CPU usage) / (resources.requests.cpu)`. Therefore, if `Deployment/shop-api` **forgets to declare ==`resources.requests.cpu`==**, the division lacks a denominator, causing HPA to report `<unknown>/70%` and completely fail to scale Pods!

steps.headingEn: Running one-off & scheduled tasks: Job and CronJob (batch/v1)
steps.bodyEn:
`Deployment` is built for 24/7 Web Servers (restarting whenever they exit). However, for short-lived tasks like **running Database Migrations (`alembic upgrade head` in Python or `prisma migrate deploy` in Node.js)**, generating end-of-day reports, or batch training data at `02:00` AM, we need a process that **finishes its job, exits with code `0` (`Completed`), and stops**:

```visual
kind: groups
title: So Sánh Job (Chạy 1 Lần) & CronJob (Lập Lịch Định Kỳ) — API batch/v1
columns: 2
items:
  - num: 1
    icon: play
    title: Job (batch/v1)
    badge: Chạy xong -> Completed
    tone: emerald
    desc: Thực thi tác vụ một lần duy nhất cho tới khi hoàn tất thành công.
    bullets:
      - "Trường `spec.template.spec.restartPolicy` **chỉ chấp nhận 2 giá trị hợp lệ là **`Never`** hoặc **`OnFailure`** (API Server từ chối thẳng giá trị mặc định `Always`!)"
      - "Dùng **`backoffLimit: 3`** để khóa số lần thử lại tối đa khi gặp lỗi mạng tạm thời, tránh lặp lỗi vô tận"
    code: |
      spec:
        backoffLimit: 3
        template:
          spec:
            restartPolicy: OnFailure
    codeLang: yaml
    footer: Chuẩn cho DB Migration (Alembic / Prisma), Seed dữ liệu
  - num: 2
    icon: refresh
    title: CronJob (batch/v1)
    badge: Unix Cron 5 trường
    tone: cyan
    desc: Tự động đẻ ra các đối tượng Job theo lịch hẹn định kỳ.
    bullets:
      - "Dùng biểu thức Cron 5 trường (`phút giờ ngày tháng thứ`, ví dụ `\"0 2 * * *\"` là 02:00 sáng hàng ngày)"
      - "Cấu hình quan trọng ==`concurrencyPolicy: Forbid`==: nếu kỳ chạy lúc 02:00 hôm nay còn chưa xong, K8s sẽ **bỏ qua kỳ kế tiếp thay vì bật chồng 2 Job chạy đè nhau**!"
    code: |
      spec:
        schedule: "0 2 * * *"
        concurrencyPolicy: Forbid
    codeLang: yaml
    footer: Ngăn khóa bảng Database hoặc gửi trùng email hàng loạt!
```

> [!REMEMBER] Key Takeaways
> - **`kube-scheduler`** reads `resources.requests` (`500m = 0.5 vCPU`) · Exceeding `limits.cpu` = **CPU Throttling** (slower but stays alive); exceeding `limits.memory` = **`OOMKilled` (`Exit Code 137`)**.
> - The highest-priority **`Guaranteed` QoS** class requires every container in the Pod to have `requests.cpu == limits.cpu` and `requests.memory == limits.memory`.
> - **HPA (`autoscaling/v2`)** strictly requires `resources.requests.cpu` · **`Job`** only allows `restartPolicy: Never | OnFailure` · **`CronJob`** uses `concurrencyPolicy: Forbid` to prevent overlapping runs.

readings.noteEn: Standard autoscaling/v2 HorizontalPodAutoscaler configuration with behavior.scaleDown policy to prevent flapping when traffic fluctuates abruptly.
readings.taskEn: Locate the stabilizationWindowSeconds field in the scaleDown section and explain its practical effect.
readings.answerEn: stabilizationWindowSeconds: 300 instructs HPA to observe consistently low load for 5 minutes (300 seconds) before scaling down Pods, avoiding a scenario where Pods are removed right before traffic spikes again and causes resource shortages.

readings.noteEn: Safe nightly backup CronJob template with concurrencyPolicy: Forbid and history retention limits for old Jobs.
readings.taskEn: Explain the role of successfulJobsHistoryLimit and failedJobsHistoryLimit in this configuration file.
readings.answerEn: They limit how many completed Job/Pod objects are retained in the cluster (for example, keeping the 3 most recent successful runs and 2 failed runs for inspecting logs), preventing etcd memory bloat after months of nightly runs.

K15-Q1.qEn: What happens differently when a container exceeds `limits.cpu` compared to when it exceeds `limits.memory`?
choicesEn: Both cases cause the container to be OOMKilled immediately

Exceeding `limits.cpu` only throttles processing speed (CPU Throttling — it stays alive), whereas exceeding `limits.memory` causes the Linux kernel to terminate it immediately with `OOMKilled` (Exit Code 137)
Exceeding `limits.memory` only slows the app down slightly while exceeding `limits.cpu` kills it
Kubernetes automatically transfers RAM from another Node over the network to the container
K15-Q1.explainEn: CPU is a compressible resource, so cgroups throttle CPU cycle speed; conversely, RAM cannot be compressed or forcibly reclaimed without corrupting memory pages, so the OOM Killer must terminate the process (Exit Code 137).

K15-Q2.qEn: How many vCPUs (virtual cores) does a CPU value of `500m` equal? (Enter a concise decimal number, e.g. `0.25`)
K15-Q2.explainEn: 1000m (1000 millicores) equals 1 full vCPU/Core, so 500m is 0.5 vCPU.

K15-Q3.qEn: For a critical Pod to be assigned the highest protection tier **`Guaranteed` QoS** by Kubernetes, how must you configure `resources`?
choicesEn: Omit the resources section completely so the Pod can use maximum server power
Declare only requests without declaring limits
Declare both CPU and Memory for every container in the Pod such that requests strictly equal limits
Set limits to 10 times requests
K15-Q3.explainEn: When every container in a Pod has requests.cpu === limits.cpu AND requests.memory === limits.memory, the Pod achieves Guaranteed QoS and is almost never evicted when the Node runs low on memory.

K15-Q4.qEn: If a `Deployment` forgets to declare `resources.requests.cpu`, a `HorizontalPodAutoscaler` scaling on CPU percentage (`averageUtilization: 70`) will still calculate usage and scale Pods normally.
K15-Q4.explainEn: False! HPA's CPU percentage divides current CPU usage by `resources.requests.cpu`. Without `requests.cpu`, the denominator is 0/undefined, causing HPA to report `<unknown>/70%` and fail to operate.

K15-Q5.qEn: In a `batch/v1` `Job` object, what are the only two valid values for `spec.template.spec.restartPolicy`?
choicesEn: `Always` and `UnlessStopped`
`Never` and `OnFailure`
`Always` and `Never`
`Immediate` and `Delayed`
K15-Q5.explainEn: Job Pods are meant to finish and stop, so the API Server outright rejects the default `Always` and only accepts `Never` (create a new Pod on failure) or `OnFailure` (restart the container in place on failure).

K15-Q6.qEn: In a `CronJob`, setting `concurrencyPolicy: Forbid` guarantees that if the previous run is still executing when the next scheduled time arrives, Kubernetes skips the new run instead of launching two concurrent Jobs.
K15-Q6.explainEn: True! `concurrencyPolicy: Forbid` is extremely useful for financial aggregation, inventory sync, or backup tasks to prevent two processes from colliding on shared data.

K15-Q7.qEn: Which Control Plane component reads `resources.requests` to choose a Worker Node with enough free capacity for a new Pod?
K15-Q7.explainEn: kube-scheduler looks strictly at `resources.requests` (the reserved baseline) to calculate which Node has enough unallocated capacity and places the Pod there.

K15-C1.frontEn: What is the difference between `resources.requests` and `resources.limits`?
K15-C1.backEn: `requests` is used by `kube-scheduler` to find a Node with enough space to place the Pod; `limits` is enforced by the Linux kernel (`cgroups`) on the Node (throttling if CPU is exceeded, killing with `OOMKilled 137` if RAM is exceeded).

K15-C2.frontEn: What is the eviction priority order of the 3 QoS classes when a Node runs out of RAM?
K15-C2.backEn: `BestEffort` (no requests/limits set) is evicted first → `Burstable` (`requests < limits`) → `Guaranteed` (`requests === limits` for both CPU & RAM) is protected until last.

K15-C3.frontEn: What are the standard conversion units for CPU and Memory in Kubernetes?
K15-C3.backEn: CPU: `1` = `1000m` (1000 millicores, `250m` = 0.25 vCPU). Memory: prefer binary units `Mi` / `Gi` (`1Gi = 1024Mi`).

K15-C4.frontEn: What is the current standard API version for `HorizontalPodAutoscaler` and its prerequisite on the Deployment?
K15-C4.backEn: `apiVersion: autoscaling/v2` (supports multiple metrics: CPU, Memory, Custom Metrics). Requires `metrics-server` in the cluster and `resources.requests` declared on the Deployment.

K15-C5.frontEn: When should you use a `Job` and what does `backoffLimit` mean?
K15-C5.backEn: Use a `batch/v1` `Job` for one-off tasks that run to completion (like DB migrations). `backoffLimit` specifies the maximum number of retries before marking the Job as failed.

K15-C6.frontEn: What do the 3 `concurrencyPolicy` options in `CronJob` (`Allow`, `Forbid`, `Replace`) mean?
K15-C6.backEn: `Allow`: allows overlapping runs; `Forbid`: skips the new schedule if the previous run has not finished; `Replace`: cancels the currently running Job to make room for the new scheduled Job.

K16.titleEn: Pod Security & Authorization: SecurityContext, Pod Security Admission & RBAC
K16.summaryEn: Harden containers to run non-root with a read-only filesystem, enforce the Pod Security Admission restricted standard replacing legacy PSP, and grant least-privilege RBAC.

steps.headingEn: Overview & Context
steps.bodyEn:
If an attacker successfully exploits a Remote Code Execution (*RCE* — e.g., via an input deserialization flaw or a compromised third-party library) inside your Python / Node.js container, what happens next?

This lesson helps you build a complete **3-layer Defense in Depth** architecture following modern 2026 Kubernetes standards (K8s v1.30+).

steps.headingEn: Defense Layer 1: Hardening securityContext at Pod and Container levels
steps.bodyEn:
In lesson `K05`, you saw `USER node` / `USER appuser` in a Dockerfile. However, Kubernetes does not blindly trust Dockerfiles (since someone could accidentally push an image forgetting the `USER` directive). We lock it down directly in YAML via **`securityContext`** at two levels:

- [x] **At the Pod level (`spec.securityContext`):** Applies across all containers and mounted volume ownership (`runAsNonRoot: true`, `runAsUser: 1000`, `fsGroup: 2000`, `seccompProfile.type: RuntimeDefault`).
- [x] **At the Container level (`spec.containers[].securityContext`):** Locks down Linux kernel privileges:
  - **`allowPrivilegeEscalation: false`:** Strictly forbids child processes from escalating privileges via `setuid` flags (`sudo`, `su`).
  - ==`capabilities.drop: ["ALL"]`==: The uppercase keyword `ALL` strips all 30+ special Linux kernel capabilities (`NET_RAW`, `SYS_ADMIN`, etc.) that a typical Web API never needs.
  - ==`readOnlyRootFilesystem: true`==: Locks the container's entire root filesystem `/` to **Read-Only**!

> [!TIP] Standard pattern for both Python & Node.js when enabling `readOnlyRootFilesystem: true`
> When locking `/` to read-only, some upload/file-processing libraries such as `python-multipart` / `tempfile` (FastAPI) or `multer` / PDF exporters (Node.js) still need to write scratch files to `/tmp`. The standard solution is to **mount a dedicated ephemeral `emptyDir: {}` volume at `/tmp`**!

```yaml
spec:
  automountServiceAccountToken: false
  securityContext:
    runAsNonRoot: true
    runAsUser: 1000
    seccompProfile:
      type: RuntimeDefault
  containers:
    - name: api
      image: ghcr.io/acme/shop-api:2.0.0
      securityContext:
        allowPrivilegeEscalation: false
        readOnlyRootFilesystem: true
        capabilities:
          drop:
            - ALL
      volumeMounts:
        - name: tmp-dir
          mountPath: /tmp
  volumes:
    - name: tmp-dir
      emptyDir: {}
```

> [!WARNING] Three backdoor-opening settings you must strictly avoid!
> Unless you are building low-level system networking infrastructure, **never use**: `privileged: true`, `hostNetwork: true`, or mounting `hostPath: /var/run/docker.sock` — because any container holding them effectively has `root` access directly on the physical host!

steps.headingEn: Defense Layer 2: Centralized enforcement with **Pod Security Admission (PSA)**
steps.bodyEn:
How do you ensure none of the 50 developers in your company forget to write `securityContext`?

Before 2022, Kubernetes used the legacy `PodSecurityPolicy` resource, which was completely removed in K8s v1.25+. Today (K8s v1.30+ / 2026), the official built-in mechanism is ==Pod Security Admission (`PSA`)== — enabled cleanly using **labels (`labels`) right on the `Namespace`** across 3 **Pod Security Standards (`PSS`)** levels:

```visual
kind: groups
title: Ba Mức Chuẩn Pod Security Standards (PSS) Của PSA [!badge:emerald:K8s v1.25+ Chuẩn Mới]
subtitle: Gắn nhãn trực tiếp trên Namespace để API Server tự động kiểm duyệt mọi Pod được tạo ra
columns: 3
items:
  - num: 1
    icon: shield-alert
    title: privileged
    badge: Mở hoàn toàn
    tone: rose
    desc: Không giới hạn đặc quyền, cho phép can thiệp sâu vào nhân máy chủ.
    bullets:
      - "Cho phép mọi quyền hệ thống ở cấp Node"
      - "Chỉ được dùng cho `kube-system`, CNI plugin mạng, hoặc agent giám sát phần cứng"
    footer: Tuyệt đối cấm dùng cho ứng dụng kinh doanh
  - num: 2
    icon: shield
    title: baseline
    badge: Chặn nguy cơ thô bạo
    tone: amber
    desc: Ngăn chặn các cấu hình leo thang nguy hiểm rõ rệt nhất.
    bullets:
      - "Cấm thẳng `privileged: true`, `hostNetwork`, `hostPID` và gắn ổ đĩa `hostPath`"
      - "Hợp cho môi trường thử nghiệm nội bộ hoặc phần mềm bên thứ ba cũ chưa kịp bỏ quyền `root`"
    footer: Mức đệm chuyển tiếp an toàn cơ bản
  - num: 3
    icon: shield-check
    title: restricted
    badge: Tiêu chuẩn vàng 2026
    tone: emerald
    desc: Thực thi khắt khe nhất mọi quy tắc gia cố chống leo thang đặc quyền.
    bullets:
      - "Bắt buộc **`runAsNonRoot: true`**, **`allowPrivilegeEscalation: false`**, **`capabilities.drop: [\"ALL\"]`** và **`seccompProfile`**!"
      - "API Server từ chối thẳng mọi Pod thiếu cấu hình bảo mật"
    footer: Khuyến nghị bắt buộc cho production, payments, orders
```

Simply by adding labels to a `Namespace`, the API Server immediately blocks non-compliant Pods (`enforce`) and surfaces early warnings (`warn`):

```yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: Namespace
metadata:
  name: payments
  labels:
    pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce: restricted
    pod-security.kubernetes.io/warn: restricted
```

steps.headingEn: Defense Layer 3: Least-privilege access with **RBAC** (ServiceAccount, Role & RoleBinding)
steps.bodyEn:
> [!NOTE] The 3 core components of RBAC
> The RBAC authorization system consists of 3 directly linked components:
> 1. **Subject (`Subject`):** For humans, this is `User`/`Group`; for applications running inside a Pod, it is **`ServiceAccount`**.
> 2. **Permission Set (`Role` vs `ClusterRole`):** Defines the list of resources (`resources`) and allowed actions (`verbs` like `get`, `list`). A `Role` applies within **1 Namespace**; a `ClusterRole` applies **cluster-wide**.
> 3. **Binding (`RoleBinding` vs `ClusterRoleBinding`):** Connects the subject in (1) to the permission set in (2). *(Think of `ServiceAccount` as the Pod's ID badge, `Role` as the permission specification sheet, and `RoleBinding` as the formal assignment granting those permissions.)*

Two non-negotiable production rules for every application:
- [!] **Rule #1 (95% of standard Web/AI APIs):** A FastAPI or Express app only talks to PostgreSQL/Redis and never calls the Kubernetes API Server → immediately set ==`automountServiceAccountToken: false`== so unnecessary token credentials aren't mounted into the Pod!
- [>] **Rule #2 (5% of internal tools that need to call the K8s API):** Apply the **Principle of Least Privilege** — **strictly forbid granting the wildcard `"*"` or supreme `cluster-admin` privileges** to an application's `ServiceAccount`!

```visual
kind: flow
title: Mô Hình 3 Mảnh Ghép Phân Quyền Tối Thiểu RBAC (Least Privilege)
subtitle: "Phân biệt rõ phạm vi 1 Namespace (Role + RoleBinding) và phạm vi toàn cụm (ClusterRole + ClusterRoleBinding)"
footer: "Kiểm tra nhanh quyền thực tế bằng lệnh: kubectl auth can-i get secrets --as=system:serviceaccount:prod:job-runner -n prod"
steps:
  - icon: key
    badge: 1. Ai gọi? (Subject)
    title: ServiceAccount (v1)
    desc: Danh tính (Identity) riêng gắn cho Pod qua trường serviceAccountName
    code: "sa: job-runner"
    tone: sky
    edge: gắn vào subjects
  - icon: workflow
    badge: 2. Quyết định bổ nhiệm
    title: RoleBinding / ClusterRoleBinding
    desc: Nối danh tính ServiceAccount (subjects) với bộ quyền hạn tương ứng (roleRef)
    code: "kind: RoleBinding"
    tone: cyan
    edge: tham chiếu roleRef
  - icon: lock
    badge: 3. Được làm gì?
    title: Role vs ClusterRole
    desc: Role chỉ hiệu lực trong 1 Namespace · ClusterRole hiệu lực toàn cụm (Nodes, PVs)
    code: 'verbs: ["get", "list"]'
    tone: emerald
    edge: kiểm duyệt tại cửa
  - icon: server
    badge: Đích đến an toàn
    title: Kubernetes API Server
    desc: Chỉ cho phép đúng thao tác đọc pods trong Namespace được cấp phép
    code: 'resources: ["pods"]'
    tone: cyan
```

> [!REMEMBER] Key Takeaways
> - **`PodSecurityPolicy` was removed in K8s v1.25**, officially replaced by **Pod Security Admission (`PSA`)** using **`restricted`**-level labels on the `Namespace`.
> - Standard container hardening: `runAsNonRoot: true`, `allowPrivilegeEscalation: false`, **`capabilities.drop: ["ALL"]`**, and `readOnlyRootFilesystem: true` (paired with an `emptyDir: {}` volume mounted at `/tmp`).
> - Disable unnecessary tokens with **`automountServiceAccountToken: false`** · Distinguish **`Role`** (single Namespace) vs **`ClusterRole`** (cluster-wide) · Strictly forbid wildcard `"*"`!

readings.noteEn: Reference configuration meeting the strictest Restricted tier of Pod Security Standards on K8s v1.30+, with a temporary emptyDir volume at /tmp.
readings.taskEn: Identify all attributes inside both securityContext blocks (Pod-level and Container-level) that enable the Pod to pass the Restricted check.
readings.answerEn: Pod-level sets runAsNonRoot: true, runAsUser: 1000, seccompProfile.type: RuntimeDefault; Container-level sets allowPrivilegeEscalation: false, capabilities.drop: ["ALL"], and readOnlyRootFilesystem: true.

readings.noteEn: An extremely dangerous YAML file that opens the door to Container Escape and full takeover of the physical host.
readings.taskEn: Point out the 3 extremely dangerous settings in this file that turn the container into root on the entire Worker Node.
readings.answerEn: 1) privileged: true (disables all cgroups/capabilities barriers), 2) hostNetwork: true (sniffs Node network traffic), and 3) mounting hostPath /var/run/docker.sock (allows creating privileged containers directly on the host).

readings.noteEn: Least-Privilege RBAC setup: disables automatic default token mounting and grants only the required read permissions scoped to a single Namespace.
readings.taskEn: Explain why RoleBinding is safer than ClusterRoleBinding when granting permissions to a single microservice.
readings.answerEn: RoleBinding restricts the permission scope strictly within a single specified Namespace (e.g., backend). Even if the Pod is compromised, an attacker cannot read resources in other Namespaces such as payments or kube-system.

K16-Q1.qEn: Since Kubernetes v1.25 (and in K8s 2026), `PodSecurityPolicy` (`policy/v1beta1`) has been completely removed and officially replaced by which built-in mechanism?
choicesEn: Docker Daemon TLS Wrapper
Pod Security Admission (PSA) applying `privileged` / `baseline` / `restricted` labels directly on the Namespace
NetworkPolicy Ingress v2
ConfigMap Security Filter
K16-Q1.explainEn: PodSecurityPolicy was removed in K8s 1.25. The official built-in replacement is Pod Security Admission (PSA), enabled via `pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce` labels on the Namespace.

K16-Q2.qEn: When enabling `readOnlyRootFilesystem: true` for a Node.js container to block malicious file writes, you can mount an `emptyDir: {}` volume at `/tmp` so the application can still write temporary files normally.
K16-Q2.explainEn: True! This is the standard design pattern: the entire source code and OS at `/` are locked immutable/read-only, while only `/tmp` backed by an ephemeral emptyDir volume is writable.

K16-Q3.qEn: To strip all unnecessary Linux kernel privileges in `securityContext.capabilities.drop`, what exact uppercase keyword must be passed in the array?
K16-Q3.explainEn: The Restricted Pod Security Standard strictly requires `capabilities.drop: ["ALL"]` to revoke all default Linux capabilities.

K16-Q4.qEn: If a standard Web API Pod has no need to communicate with the Kubernetes API Server, which setting prevents leaking the cluster's internal auth token inside the container?
choicesEn: Set `automountServiceAccountToken: false` on the ServiceAccount or Pod spec
Set `restartPolicy: Never`
Change the `Service` to `ClusterIP: None`
Remove `containerPort` from the Deployment
K16-Q4.explainEn: By default, K8s mounts a token file at `/var/run/secrets/kubernetes.io/serviceaccount/token` in every Pod. Setting `automountServiceAccountToken: false` completely disables this unnecessary token mount.

K16-Q5.qEn: What is the core difference between `Role` and `ClusterRole` in Kubernetes RBAC?
choicesEn: `Role` is for humans while `ClusterRole` is only for machines
`Role` applies only within a specific Namespace, whereas `ClusterRole` is cluster-wide (including non-namespaced resources like Nodes and PersistentVolumes)
`Role` only allows reading (`get`), while `ClusterRole` allows deleting (`delete`)
`Role` was deprecated in K8s 1.28
K16-Q5.explainEn: Role is a Namespaced resource, whereas ClusterRole is a Cluster-scoped resource.

K16-Q6.qEn: Granting `verbs: ["*"]` and `resources: ["*"]` (or `cluster-admin`) to the `default` ServiceAccount helps microservices run smoothly and is the recommended secure configuration for Production.
K16-Q6.explainEn: Seriously false! Granting wildcard `*` / `cluster-admin` to an application ServiceAccount means any RCE vulnerability in Node.js code lets an attacker wipe or steal every Secret across the entire K8s cluster!

K16-Q7.qEn: Among the three Pod Security Standards levels (`privileged`, `baseline`, `restricted`), which level is the strictest and recommended for Namespaces running production payment applications?
K16-Q7.explainEn: The `restricted` level enforces the strictest security hardening standards against privilege escalation in Production.

K16-C1.frontEn: What are the four core `securityContext` attributes required for a Pod to pass the `restricted` security standard?

K16-C2.frontEn: How do you enable `readOnlyRootFilesystem: true` without breaking a Node.js app that needs to write temp files?
K16-C2.backEn: Declare `volumes: [{ name: tmp, emptyDir: {} }]` on the Pod and attach `volumeMounts: [{ name: tmp, mountPath: /tmp }]` to the container.

K16-C3.frontEn: How does Pod Security Admission (PSA) work to replace legacy PodSecurityPolicy?
K16-C3.backEn: Add labels directly onto the `Namespace`, such as `pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce: restricted`, so the API Server automatically rejects non-compliant Pods.

K16-C4.frontEn: What are the three pieces that form a complete RBAC authorization setup for a Pod in a Namespace?

K16-C5.frontEn: Why should you set `automountServiceAccountToken: false` for most Web/API Pods?
K16-C5.backEn: Prevents K8s from automatically mounting a JWT token file inside the container; if the app suffers an arbitrary file read (LFI/RCE) flaw, the attacker still cannot steal a token to probe the API Server.

K16-C6.frontEn: What are the three "forbidden" settings on application Pods because they enable container escape to the physical host?
K16-C6.backEn: `privileged: true`, `hostNetwork: true` / `hostPID: true`, and mounting sensitive `hostPath` volumes (especially `/var/run/docker.sock` or `/etc`).

kube-ex-k16-1.titleEn: Harden securityContext to run Non-Root and drop Linux Capabilities
kube-ex-k16-1.promptEn:
The `auth-service` Pod currently runs unrestricted with dangerous defaults. Harden `securityContext` at both levels:

1. Pod level (`spec.securityContext`): set `runAsNonRoot: true` and `runAsUser: 1000`.
2. Container level (`spec.containers[0].securityContext`): set `allowPrivilegeEscalation: false` and include `"ALL"` in `capabilities.drop`.
hintsEn: Notice there are 2 `securityContext` blocks: one directly under `spec:`, and one inside the `- name: auth` element under `containers:`.
In YAML, `true` and `false` are booleans (do not wrap them in quotes).

kube-ex-k16-2.titleEn: Lock root filesystem read-only with an emptyDir scratch volume at /tmp
kube-ex-k16-2.promptEn:
To completely prevent attackers from downloading and writing malware to disk inside the `invoice-worker` container:

1. Enable `readOnlyRootFilesystem: true` inside `spec.containers[0].securityContext`.
2. Declare a scratch volume at `spec.volumes[0]` with `name: tmp-vol` and `emptyDir: {}`.
3. Mount `spec.containers[0].volumeMounts[0]` (`name: tmp-vol`) at `mountPath: /tmp` so the Node.js PDF library can still create temporary files.
hintsEn: Explicitly write curly braces `emptyDir: {}` (a valid empty object in YAML) rather than leaving it blank after the colon!

kube-ex-k16-3.titleEn: Enforce Pod Security Admission restricted level on the payments Namespace
kube-ex-k16-3.promptEn:
The Security Team requires all Pods deployed into the `payments` `Namespace` to be automatically validated against the strictest **`restricted`** standard of **Pod Security Admission**.

Complete the `payments` `Namespace` (`apiVersion: v1`) with two labels under `metadata.labels`:
- `pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce: restricted`
- `pod-security.kubernetes.io/warn: restricted`
hintsEn: Double-check the exact standard K8s prefix: `pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce: restricted` and `pod-security.kubernetes.io/warn: restricted`.

kube-ex-k16-4.titleEn: Tighten an RBAC Role to remove dangerous Wildcard (*) permissions
kube-ex-k16-4.promptEn:
A lazy developer wrote the `pod-reader` `Role` in the `backend` namespace using the wildcard `"*"`, which allows wiping out all Secrets and Deployments!

Fix the `Role` (`apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1`) according to the **Principle of Least Privilege**:
- `rules[0].apiGroups: [""]` (Core API group)
- `rules[0].resources: ["pods"]` (read-only access to `pods`, strictly no `"*"`)
- `rules[0].verbs: ["get", "list", "watch"]` (only these 3 read actions, no `"*"` or `"delete"`)
hintsEn: In RBAC, core resources like `pods`, `services`, and `configmaps` belong to the Core API group, so `apiGroups` is written as `[""]` (an array with an empty string).

kube-ex-k16-5.titleEn: Bind a ServiceAccount to a Role using a multi-document RoleBinding
kube-ex-k16-5.promptEn:
Complete the multi-document YAML file (`---`) in the `backend` namespace to bind the `job-runner` `ServiceAccount` identity to the `config-reader` `Role`:

1. Document 1 (`ServiceAccount` named `job-runner`, `namespace: backend`) and Document 2 (`Role` named `config-reader`, `namespace: backend`) are already provided.
2. Complete Document 3 (`RoleBinding` named `job-runner-binding`, `namespace: backend`, `apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1`):
   - `subjects[0]`: `kind: ServiceAccount`, `name: job-runner`, `namespace: backend`
   - `roleRef`: `apiGroup: rbac.authorization.k8s.io`, `kind: Role`, `name: config-reader`
hintsEn: Fill in `subjects[0].name: job-runner` (who receives the permissions) and `roleRef.name: config-reader` (which permission bundle is granted).

K17.titleEn: Network Isolation with NetworkPolicy & Packaging with Helm / Kustomize
K17.summaryEn: Lock down the default flat network using NetworkPolicy (Default Deny & Whitelist) and compare multi-environment configuration management between Helm Charts and Kustomize (kubectl apply -k).

steps.headingEn: Overview & Context
steps.bodyEn:
You have come a very long way: from container packaging, zero-downtime Deployments, and Service/Gateway API routing to PVC storage management, `securityContext` hardening, and RBAC. In the final stage of Level 5, we solve two major architectural challenges before moving into large-scale enterprise operations:

- [!] **Internal networking:** By default in Kubernetes, the cluster network is completely flat — how do you stop a compromised Frontend Pod from connecting directly to PostgreSQL port `5432`?
- [!] **Multi-environment configuration management:** When a single service requires 8 YAML manifests (`Deployment`, `Service`, `HTTPRoute`, `HPA`, `ConfigMap`, `ServiceAccount`, `NetworkPolicy`, etc.) multiplied across 4 environments (`dev`, `qa`, `staging`, `prod`), how do you escape manually copying dozens of nearly identical YAML files?

The answer is the internal firewall ==`NetworkPolicy`== paired with the 2026 industry-standard configuration duo: ==`Helm`== and ==`Kustomize`==!

```visual
kind: illustration
diagram: "kube:k17"
alt: "Tường lửa mạng nội bộ Zero-Trust với NetworkPolicy (Default Deny + Whitelist + DNS Egress 53) và bộ máy đóng gói biểu mẫu Helm Chart"
title: "Cơ Chế NetworkPolicy (Zero-Trust) & Đóng Gói Cấu Hình Helm / Kustomize"
subtitle: "Khóa chặt lưu lượng ngang Đông-Tây giữa các tầng dịch vụ và tái sử dụng một bộ khuôn mẫu YAML duy nhất cho mọi môi trường"
caption: "Mô hình tường lửa Pod-to-Pod thực thi bởi Cilium/Calico (nhớ mở cổng 53 cho CoreDNS) và quy trình kết xuất cấu hình đa môi trường"
callouts:
  - num: 1
    label: "Zero-Trust NetworkPolicy: Khóa mặc định & Mở chọn lọc"
    desc: "Áp dụng default-deny (podSelector: {}) chặn 100% kết nối lạ, sau đó chỉ mở đúng luồng hợp lệ từ web -> api -> postgres:5432."
    tone: emerald
  - num: 2
    label: "Lưu ý quan trọng khi khóa chiều ra (Egress) — Cổng 53 DNS"
    desc: "Khi bật kiểm soát Egress, luôn phải mở cổng UDP/TCP 53 sang kube-system để Pod không bị mù phân giải tên miền CoreDNS."
    tone: cyan
  - num: 3
    label: "Helm & Kustomize — Chuẩn hóa triển khai GitOps"
    desc: "Dùng Helm Chart (khuôn mẫu + values.yaml) hoặc Kustomize (kubectl apply -k) để đồng bộ sạch sẽ qua ArgoCD / Flux."
    tone: cyan
```

steps.headingEn: NetworkPolicy isolation mechanism: Default-Deny and Whitelist principles
steps.bodyEn:
> [!NOTE] Kubernetes networking allows all Pods to communicate by default (`Allow-All`)
> Many people mistakenly assume splitting into `Namespaces` (`marketing` and `production`) automatically isolates the network. In reality, **Namespaces only separate resource names, not network firewalls** — by default, without a `NetworkPolicy`, any Pod in any Namespace can directly reach the IP/port of any other Pod.
> **`NetworkPolicy`** defines Layer 3/4 (IP/Port) firewall rules for Pods: you apply a rule blocking all connections by default (`Default Deny`), then selectively open only valid paths from `web` → `api` and `api` → `postgres:5432` (much like installing keycard access doors between departments inside an open building).

```visual
kind: compare
title: "Mạng Phẳng Mặc Định (Allow All) vs Tường Lửa Zero-Trust (NetworkPolicy)"
subtitle: "Cô lập kết nối ở tầng IP/Port (Layer 3 / Layer 4) dựa trên nhãn (Labels) của Pod"
left:
  badge: "MẶC ĐỊNH K8S · Mở Toang 100%"
```
